slides: So, a quick summary before you practice on your own.
Everything we learned about new operations... in about three minutes.
A new operation is just a definition. So read it first, and then follow the whole recipe.
Whatever sits before the symbol goes into a. Whatever sits after it goes into b.
And don't assume it behaves like plus. If you swap the inputs, you can get a different answer.
So circle which number goes into which slot.
Whatever goes in, goes in brackets. Every time.
Minus four, in brackets, squared, is sixteen. Without brackets, you'd get minus sixteen.
An expression goes in the same way. The whole thing, in brackets... and then you open them.
Inside a longer exercise? First turn every operation into a plain number. Then do the rest.
An operation inside an operation? You go inside out.
The result of the inside becomes the input of the outside. And don't stop halfway... the halfway number is waiting for you in the choices.
Now, here the rule works on three t. Not on t.
So first match the whole input. Three t is eighteen, so t is six. Then the rule gives thirteen.
If you put eighteen straight into t, you're really calculating F of fifty-four.
No definition at all? Put the given input into each choice. The one that doesn't give the result is out.
Found it? Mark it, and move on.
An unknown input? Write the definition... and it's just an ordinary equation.
Or work back from the answers. Put each choice into the rule.
Only a property? Put each rule on trial with a test value. Not zero or one.
A step property? Test two neighbors.
Two families undo themselves: c minus x, and c over x. Squares and doubling never do.
An inverse operation? Undo the steps in reverse order, and then check with one number.
Two rules? Check the input first. Is it odd, or even?
And check again at every step. The output of one step is the next input, and it can switch.
The result is given? Try every rule. But keep an answer only if it fits the rule you used.
The operation inside its own definition? Go down to the start value. Then climb back up with real numbers.
The operation on both sides? Treat it as the unknown, and isolate it.
And a definition in words? Write two or three examples first.
To say no, you need one example. To say yes, you need algebra.
Zero, one, and equal values can make a false rule look true. Two choices left? Try a second number.
And well... a must-be-true question can eat your time. Skip it, and come back at the end.
One shortcut from the advanced questions: a number minus its opposite. The even powers cancel.
So, before every question, ask yourself:
The traps: minus four squared without brackets, stopping halfway in a nested operation, and putting the number straight into t.
Read the definition, and follow it faithfully. Good luck.
